front_matter.disclaimer: This book documents construction methods, geometric principles, experimental designs, and prototype concepts. It is not a substitute for site-specific structural engineering. Building codes, loads, materials, soil conditions, permitting requirements, electrical rules, plumbing rules, and fire-safety requirements vary by location. Structural designs intended for permanent occupancy should be reviewed for the applicable site, loads, materials, connections, foundation, and local requirements by appropriately qualified professionals and authorities.
front_matter.introduction:
A geodesic dome looks complicated until you stop looking at the whole dome.

From a distance it looks like a curved structure made from dozens of parts pointing in different directions. Up close, it becomes something much simpler. It is a collection of straight pieces arranged into triangles.

That difference is important.

The dome looks curved, but the individual structural members do not have to be curved. A builder can create a large rounded structure using straight pieces of lumber, repeatable cuts, and a relatively small number of different part dimensions.

Most geodesic dome systems solve the problem of connecting those pieces with some type of hub, plate, bracket, flattened strut end, or specially manufactured connector.

The wedge method approaches the problem differently.

Instead of treating the strut as a rectangular member that must somehow be forced into the geometry of the dome, the shape of the structural member itself becomes part of that geometry.

The member is cut as a wedge.

The narrow portion of the wedge faces toward the inside of the dome and the wider portion faces toward the outside. When the members are arranged into triangles and the triangles begin joining one another, the changing thickness of the members helps create the angular relationship between neighboring faces.

This does not eliminate geometry. It uses geometry.

That distinction is the basis of this book.

The purpose of this book is not to describe one dome with one set of measurements. The goal is to explain a method of building geodesic structures so that the builder understands what the parts are doing, how they can be produced, how the system can be scaled, and how different construction approaches can grow from the same basic idea.

Some versions may begin with ordinary dimensional lumber. Others may begin with larger timbers. A builder with access to logs may choose to divide the log longitudinally and recover multiple wedge-shaped structural members from the same piece of wood.

Other versions could use laminated members, manufactured components, metal reinforcement, removable panels, insulated shells, or entirely different enclosure systems.

The frame and the enclosure also do not necessarily have to be treated as the same thing.

A structural dome can support plywood panels, fiberglass panels, transparent panels, insulated composite panels, or a removable shell. Doors and windows can be introduced by reinforcing openings in the triangular structure. Utilities can enter through the floor, through a dedicated service location, or through a central utility system.

Once the geometry and construction method are understood, the dome stops being one particular building and becomes a platform.

That is where this book is headed.

We will begin with the basic geometry of the dome and the wedge-shaped structural member. From there we will move through material selection, fabrication, repetitive cutting, connections, assembly, foundations, panels, openings, utilities, and several variations of the system.

A reference dome will be used throughout the book so that the geometry does not remain abstract. The same principles will then be scaled and modified to show how the method can be applied to structures of different sizes and purposes.

Some information in this book is mathematical. Some comes from fabrication and construction. Some sections explore design possibilities that may require additional testing or engineering before being used in an occupied structure.

Those categories will be identified rather than treated as if they are the same thing.

A dome intended to hold tools is not necessarily designed to the same requirements as a permanent residence. Snow, wind, soil, foundations, fasteners, fire safety, electrical systems, plumbing systems, and local building requirements can all change what is acceptable for a particular project.

This book therefore focuses on understanding and constructing the system rather than replacing project-specific structural engineering or local code requirements.

The basic idea, however, is simple:

Start with straight material.

Understand the triangle.

Shape the member to participate in the geometry.

Repeat the part accurately.

Connect the triangles.

And allow many simple pieces to become one structure.

sections.title: What a geodesic dome is
sections.body:
A geodesic dome is a rounded structure built from a network of straight members.

That is the first thing to understand about it.

The finished structure may look curved, but the individual pieces making up the frame do not have to be curved. Instead, straight members are connected into a repeating network of triangles. As more of those triangles are joined together at slightly different angles, the overall frame begins to follow the shape of a sphere.

In practical terms, we are using a collection of flat triangular faces to approximate a curved surface.

A simple way to picture this is to imagine replacing the smooth surface of a ball with a large number of flat panels. A ball made from only a few large flat faces would look obviously angular. Divide those faces into smaller pieces and the shape begins to look progressively rounder.

A geodesic dome works on the same basic idea.

The frame is not one continuous curved beam. It is a collection of straight structural members whose lengths and connection geometry place them at the correct points in space.

This matters to a builder because straight pieces are much easier to produce repeatedly than large curved ones.

A saw can cut another member to the same length.

A jig can hold another piece in the same position.

A stop can reproduce a cut.

A template can reproduce a panel.

The finished building may have a complicated three-dimensional shape, while much of the actual fabrication is reduced to making the same small group of parts over and over.

GEOMETRY

A complete sphere can be described using points, straight lines between those points, and the triangular faces created by those lines. A dome uses only part of that spherical structure.

The exact portion of the sphere used depends on the design.

Some domes are approximately hemispherical. Others stop above or below the halfway point. A dome may also be placed on a vertical wall, a raised base, or another supporting structure.

For that reason, saying that two structures are both "geodesic domes" does not mean they automatically use the same strut lengths, number of triangles, base shape, or connection angles.

The underlying geometry matters.

The frequency of the dome also matters. Frequency describes how far the original triangular faces used to develop the sphere have been subdivided. A higher-frequency dome generally contains more members and smaller triangular faces.

The full frequency calculations and the exact strut families used in this book are covered later. For now, the important point is that the rounded shape is produced by a calculated arrangement of straight pieces rather than by bending the frame into a curve.

The reference structure used throughout this book is a 20-foot-diameter 2V dome.

That description tells us two useful things.

The 20-foot dimension tells us the intended diameter of the reference structure.

The 2V designation tells us the frequency of the geodesic subdivision.

It does not, by itself, tell us every dimension needed to build the dome. The exact sphere geometry, truncation, base configuration, strut lengths, and joint geometry still have to be defined before a reliable cut list can be produced.

That distinction is important throughout this book.

A drawing that looks like a 2V dome is not enough information to start cutting lumber.

The geometry has to be established first.

THE WEDGE METHOD

The wedge method does not change the basic definition of a geodesic dome.

We still have straight members forming triangular faces and those faces joining together to create a rounded three-dimensional structure.

What changes is the shape of the structural member and the way we use that shape at the joints.

A conventional wood dome can begin with rectangular lumber. The builder then has to deal with the fact that neighboring triangular faces do not all lie in the same plane. Their edges meet at angles.

Different dome systems handle that problem in different ways. They may use metal hubs, flattened pipe ends, plates, brackets, compound cuts, flexible connections, or other hardware.

The wedge method approaches the same three-dimensional problem by making the cross-section of the timber itself part of the system.

Instead of every member remaining rectangular from its inside face to its outside face, the member is formed as a wedge.

The narrow portion is oriented toward the interior of the dome and the wider portion toward the exterior.

When those members are assembled into the frame, the wedge shape becomes part of how neighboring faces transition around the curved surface.

That does not mean the wedge automatically determines every connection angle.

It also does not mean that any wedge-shaped piece of lumber can be assembled into a dome.

The strut lengths, triangle geometry, vertex arrangement, member orientation, and connection details still have to agree with one another.

The useful idea is that the shape of the timber can participate in the three-dimensional geometry instead of being treated only as a straight rectangular stick that needs separate hardware to resolve every change in direction.

From a builder's point of view, this gives us two geometries to think about.

The first is the geometry of the dome itself: where every vertex and strut belongs in space.

The second is the geometry of the individual wedge member: its width, thickness, taper, orientation, end treatment, and connection to the neighboring pieces.

The rest of the method comes from making those two geometries work together.

This is also why the wedge method can have several variations.

The starting material could be dimensional lumber.

It could be larger sawn timber.

It could be material recovered from a log by dividing the log longitudinally into usable wedge-shaped sections.

A wedge could be solid, laminated, reinforced, or incorporated into a larger panel system.

Those are different fabrication strategies built around the same basic idea.

DESIGN VARIATION

The frame should also be thought of separately from the outer shell.

A geodesic frame defines the structural geometry. What is attached to that frame can vary.

A dome might use plywood triangles, fiberglass panels, sheet material, transparent sections, insulation assemblies, removable panels, or another enclosure system.

That distinction becomes useful later because changing the enclosure does not necessarily require changing the entire geometric system underneath it.

The same is true for floors, foundations, doors, windows, and utility routing. These systems have to interact with the dome, but they are not what makes the structure geodesic.

At its simplest, the dome can be understood as a three-dimensional framework of calculated straight members.

Everything else is built around that framework.

For this book, that gives us a useful order of operations.

First we establish the dome geometry.

Then we determine what the wedge-shaped member has to do inside that geometry.

Then we work out how to manufacture those members repeatedly.

After that, we can deal with the connections, assembly sequence, openings, shell, floor, foundation, utilities, and the different ways the same basic system can be modified.

The dome may look complicated when viewed as one complete object.

For fabrication, we will break it back down into individual parts.

That is where the system becomes manageable.

sections.title: Why triangles are used
sections.body:
Triangles are used because three connected sides can define a shape without needing another member to keep that shape from folding sideways.

That makes them useful anywhere we want a frame to hold a predictable geometry.

Take four straight pieces and connect them into a rectangle.

If the corners are allowed to rotate, the rectangle can lean sideways and become a parallelogram without changing the length of any of the four sides.

Nothing has to stretch.

Nothing has to get shorter.

The joints only have to rotate.

Now add a diagonal brace across that rectangle.

The diagonal divides it into two triangles.

At that point, changing the shape requires one or more of the member lengths to change, a connection to slip, or a member to bend.

That is the basic reason triangular framing appears throughout a geodesic dome.

GEOMETRY

A triangle is determined by its geometry in a way that a four-sided frame is not.

If we know the lengths of all three sides of a valid triangle, its angles are also determined.

For sides \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\), the angle \(C\) opposite side \(c\) can be found with the law of cosines:

$$
c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos(C)
$$

Rearranging it gives:

$$
C = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}\right)
$$

The other two angles can be calculated the same way.

This matters in a dome because the strut lengths are not just pieces we cut to fill space. Their lengths establish the triangular faces.

Once those lengths are correct, the triangle has a defined shape.

The next problem is then how that triangle meets the triangles around it in three-dimensional space.

That second problem is where the dome's curvature appears.

The individual triangle can be treated as a flat geometric face.

The neighboring triangle is also a flat face.

The angle between those two faces turns the collection of flat triangles into a rounded structure.

A dome is therefore not made by bending each triangle.

The curvature comes from changing the orientation of one triangle relative to the next.

For the wedge method, that distinction is especially useful.

We can first think about the geometry inside one triangular face:

* What are its three side lengths?
* Which strut family forms each side?
* What are its three internal angles?
* Is it equilateral, isosceles, or scalene?

Then we deal with the three-dimensional relationship between that face and the faces beside it.

The wedge-shaped member is part of solving that second problem.

TRIANGLES AS REPEATABLE BUILDING UNITS

From a fabrication standpoint, triangles also give us manageable units.

Instead of trying to position every member of the dome independently in open space, we can think in terms of repeated triangular relationships.

If a dome uses two triangle types, for example, we do not have to invent forty different shapes just because the finished dome contains forty triangular faces.

We identify the repeating geometry and make those parts consistently.

This is one of the places where geodesic construction begins to make more sense from a builder's point of view.

The finished frame is complicated.

The list of unique parts may not be.

A group of accurately repeated strut lengths can produce a much larger three-dimensional form when those struts are assembled in the correct pattern.

The triangle becomes the bridge between those two scales.

At the fabrication scale, we are cutting individual pieces.

At the assembly scale, those pieces become triangles.

At the building scale, the triangles become the dome.

WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE WEDGE METHOD

In a conventional rectangular timber frame, the member is usually treated as having the same basic cross-section from one end to the other.

The connection hardware or the end cuts then have to deal with how one face of the structure changes direction relative to another.

The wedge method gives us another variable to work with.

The member itself has a narrow side and a wide side.

When the narrow side is oriented toward the interior and the wider side toward the exterior, the cross-section can participate in the transition between neighboring triangular faces.

The triangle is still defined by its strut geometry.

The wedge does not replace that geometry.

It changes how we can physically realize that geometry in timber.

This means there are several different angles in the system that should not be confused with one another.

There are the internal angles inside a triangular face.

There are the angles created where struts meet at a vertex.

There are the angles between neighboring triangular faces.

There are also the angles created by the wedge-shaped cross-section of the timber itself.

They are related, but they are not interchangeable.

A common mistake would be to calculate one of those angles and assume it is automatically the saw setting needed for another part of the joint.

We will keep them separate throughout the book.

REFERENCE BUILD

The 20-foot-diameter 2V reference dome will contain repeating triangular faces made from the strut families established by its exact geodesic geometry.

Once those strut lengths are formally defined, we can calculate the internal angles of each triangle directly from their side lengths.

For a triangular face with verified side lengths \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\), the calculation will be:

$$
C = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}\right)
$$

That gives the flat internal angle of the triangle.

It does not yet give us the angle between that triangle and the neighboring face.

That relationship is handled separately when we get into the three-dimensional dome geometry and the wedge itself.

This separation is important because it keeps the fabrication logic clean.

First determine the correct strut lengths.

Then verify the triangle.

Then determine how the triangles meet.

Then determine what the wedge member has to do at those connections.

If we mix those steps together, it becomes much easier to cut the right number at the wrong angle.

For now, the main point is simple:

Triangles let us create repeatable, fixed geometric units from straight members.

The dome comes from arranging those units correctly in three-dimensional space.

sections.title: Chords versus curved surfaces
sections.body:
A dome may follow a curved surface, but the timber member between two connection points is straight.

That difference is where the chord comes in.

If we mark two points on a circle or sphere, there are two basic ways to describe the distance between them.

One is to follow the curved surface.

The other is to connect the two points directly with a straight line.

That straight line is a chord.

GEOMETRY

For dome construction, the structural member normally follows the chord between two vertices rather than following the curved surface of the sphere.

If two points on a circle are separated by a central angle \(\theta\), and the sphere or circle has radius \(R\), the straight chord length between those points is:

$$
c = 2R\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)
$$

where:

* \(c\) is the straight chord length,
* \(R\) is the radius,
* and \(\theta\) is the central angle between the two points.

The curved distance along the circle between the same two points is the arc length:

$$
s = R\theta
$$

when \(\theta\) is measured in radians.

Those two distances are not the same.

The arc follows the curve.

The chord cuts straight across between the endpoints.

For any normal dome segment, the chord is shorter than the arc connecting the same two points.

That matters because we are cutting straight structural members.

If a calculator gives us the spherical surface distance but we cut a straight timber to that number, the member will be too long for the chord it is supposed to occupy.

The dome geometry therefore has to distinguish between the mathematical sphere we are approximating and the straight pieces we are actually building from.

STRAIGHT MEMBERS, CURVED RESULT

A geodesic dome does not need its struts bent into the spherical radius.

Each individual strut is straight.

The curved form appears because the endpoints of those straight struts are positioned on or near the intended spherical geometry.

A single triangle is flat.

The triangle beside it is also flat.

But the two triangles do not remain in the same plane.

They meet at an angle.

Repeat that relationship over many faces and the collection of flat triangles begins to surround a volume that approximates part of a sphere.

This gives us three different things that are easy to accidentally treat as one:

1. the ideal curved sphere,
2. the flat triangular faces approximating that sphere,
3. the straight structural members forming the edges of those faces.

They are related, but they are not geometrically identical.

A drawing of a smooth sphere represents the intended overall surface.

A geodesic frame replaces that smooth surface with flat triangular facets.

The timber then forms the straight edges of those facets.

THE GAP BETWEEN A CHORD AND THE CURVE

We can also describe how far a chord falls inside the ideal curved surface.

For a circular section, the maximum distance between a chord and the corresponding arc occurs at the midpoint of the chord.

That distance is commonly called the sagitta.

If the radius is \(R\) and the chord length is \(c\), it can be calculated as:

$$
h = R-\sqrt{R^2-\left(\frac{c}{2}\right)^2}
$$

where:

* \(h\) is the sagitta,
* \(R\) is the radius,
* and \(c\) is the chord length.

This gives us a useful way to think about frequency.

Longer chords create larger flat facets across the curved surface.

Shorter chords generally reduce the distance between each flat facet and the ideal spherical surface.

That is one reason increasing frequency makes the finished form appear smoother.

We are not making the members curved.

We are using more, smaller straight sections to approximate the curve more closely.

WHY THIS MATTERS WHEN BUILDING

This distinction affects more than the mathematical drawing.

It affects where the shell sits.

It affects how neighboring panels meet.

It affects the outer profile of the dome.

It can also affect how we define the diameter.

Suppose somebody says they are building a 20-foot dome.

That sounds specific, but we still need to know what surface the 20 feet refers to.

It could mean:

* the diameter through the theoretical spherical vertex locations,
* the outside face of the structural frame,
* the inside face of the structural frame,
* the outer surface of the enclosure,
* or another construction reference.

Those numbers do not have to be identical once the frame has real thickness.

For mathematical work, the cleanest starting point is usually a defined spherical radius and a defined set of vertex locations.

Physical timber dimensions can then be developed around that geometry.

The alternative is dangerous: allowing the thickness of the material to silently change the geometry while still using calculations based on another radius.

THE WEDGE METHOD AND THE SPHERICAL SURFACE

This distinction becomes particularly important with wedge-shaped members.

A rectangular strut has parallel major faces.

A wedge member does not.

Its cross-section changes from a narrow interior side to a wider exterior side.

Because of that, we need to be explicit about which line through the member corresponds to the calculated geodesic chord.

Possible reference lines could include the interior edge, exterior edge, centerline, fastener centerline, or another deliberately chosen construction datum.

They cannot all represent the exact same spherical radius.

If the calculated chord is based on vertex centerlines but the physical cut length is measured along the outside edge of a thick wedge, those two measurements may differ.

That does not mean the geometry is wrong.

It means the mathematical model and the physical member are being measured from different references.

The solution is to establish one reference system and keep using it.

For example, the geometry may define every vertex from a common spherical center and establish each theoretical strut as the straight chord between those vertices.

The physical wedge can then be positioned around that theoretical line according to the joint design.

Once that relationship is fixed, other dimensions can be derived from it instead of being guessed independently.

This is particularly useful when we start generating cut lists.

A cut list should not simply say:

"A strut = this long."

It should eventually make clear what that dimension represents.

Is it:

* theoretical vertex-to-vertex chord length,
* bolt-center distance,
* full timber length before end cuts,
* finished timber length,
* inside-edge length,
* or outside-edge length?

If we do not define that reference, two builders can use the same number and still manufacture different parts.

REFERENCE BUILD

For the 20-foot-diameter 2V reference dome, the process will be:

First, define exactly what the 20-foot diameter refers to.

Then establish the radius:

$$
R=\frac{D}{2}
$$

If the defined mathematical diameter is 20 feet, then:

$$
R=10\text{ ft}
$$

or:

$$
R=120\text{ in}
$$

That radius alone is not enough to calculate every member.

We still need the verified angular relationship between each pair of neighboring vertices in the selected 2V geometry.

Once a central angle \(\theta\) for a particular strut family is known, its theoretical chord can be calculated from:

$$
c = 2R\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)
$$

That gives us the straight geometric distance between those vertices.

The physical wedge member can then be developed from that chord according to the connection method and whichever construction reference line we decide to use.

This order matters.

We should not begin with the outside surface of a piece of lumber and try to make the spherical geometry conform to it afterward.

We establish the geometry first.

Then we decide how the real material fits around it.

That keeps the ideal dome, the straight chord, and the finished wedge member as three separate but connected parts of the same system.

sections.title: Traditional strut/hub construction
sections.body:
Traditional geodesic dome construction usually treats the struts and the hubs as two separate parts of the system.

The struts establish the distances between vertices.

The hubs solve the problem of bringing several struts together at one point in three-dimensional space.

That separation is useful because it lets the strut itself remain relatively simple.

A strut can be a piece of wood, tube, pipe, angle, or another straight structural member.

The complicated directional change happens at the hub.

In practical terms, a hub is the connection point where several members meet.

Depending on the dome geometry, a hub may receive five, six, or another number of struts.

Those struts do not all approach from one flat plane.

They arrive from different directions because each one belongs to a different triangular face of the dome.

The hub has to accommodate that three-dimensional relationship.

TRADITIONAL HUB LOGIC

A simple flat frame can be bolted together through one plate because the members may all lie in nearly the same plane.

A dome is different.

At a dome vertex, the neighboring triangles wrap around the surface.

That means the struts meeting at the vertex point outward in different directions.

A connection system has to deal with two basic things:

1. where the end of each strut belongs,
2. what direction each strut leaves the vertex.

The mathematical geometry can define those directions precisely.

The physical hub then has to reproduce them closely enough for the structure to assemble.

Different dome systems solve this in different ways.

Some use a central metal hub with separate tabs or arms.

Some flatten the ends of metal tubing and bolt the flattened ends together.

Some use steel plates on one or both sides of wood members.

Some use pipe sections, rings, fabricated sockets, brackets, or custom-machined connectors.

The exact hardware changes, but the general idea is the same:

Keep the long structural members relatively simple and concentrate the connection geometry at the vertices.

STRUT LENGTH AND HUB GEOMETRY ARE RELATED

The geometric chord between two theoretical vertices is not always the same dimension as the physical piece of material that gets cut.

That depends on the connection design.

Suppose two theoretical vertices are separated by a chord length \(c\).

If a hub occupies some physical distance at each end of that chord, the strut may stop short of the actual vertex location.

A simple conceptual relationship is:

$$
L_{physical}=c-e_1-e_2
$$

where:

* \(L_{physical}\) is the physical member length between its connection interfaces,
* \(c\) is the theoretical vertex-to-vertex chord,
* \(e_1\) is the connection offset at one end,
* \(e_2\) is the connection offset at the other end.

That is not a universal dome-cutting formula.

It is a reminder that the connector has physical size.

If the connection reference is bolt center to bolt center instead, then the useful shop dimension may be the distance between bolt centers rather than the overall timber length.

This is why dome plans need to state what their strut dimensions actually measure.

A list of numbers without a connection reference can be misleading.

HUBS AS GEOMETRY CONVERTERS

One useful way to think about a hub is as a geometry converter.

The strut itself may be a rectangular piece of lumber.

The dome around it is not rectangular.

The hub sits between those two conditions.

It lets a straight member with a simple cross-section participate in a structure where neighboring members leave the connection at different angles.

That can make fabrication easier in one part of the project.

Instead of shaping every long member to resolve the three-dimensional joint, we manufacture or purchase a connector designed to do it.

The tradeoff is that the connector becomes a specialized component.

Now the build depends on both the struts and the hubs being correct.

If the strut lengths are right but the hub geometry is wrong, the dome will not fit correctly.

If the hub is right but the struts are cut to the wrong reference length, the same problem occurs.

The connection system and the chord geometry have to be treated as one coordinated design.

WOOD STRUTS WITH METAL HUBS

For timber domes, one common approach is to keep the wood members rectangular and attach their ends to metal hardware.

The hardware can provide:

* a bolt location,
* spacing between members,
* rotational freedom during assembly,
* a defined connection angle,
* and reinforcement around the joint.

This can simplify the wood fabrication.

Instead of cutting a complicated three-dimensional joint into every timber, the builder may only need to cut struts to length, drill them accurately, and attach the hardware.

That is a strong manufacturing advantage when the hub system is already available and correctly designed.

It also introduces another manufacturing problem.

The hubs themselves now have to be bought or made.

If the dome uses several different vertex conditions, the connector system may need multiple hub types, different tab angles, or enough flexibility to accommodate those differences.

That means the structure may have only a few strut families but still require a carefully organized connection inventory.

ASSEMBLY WITH HUBS

Hub systems can also change the assembly process.

Individual struts can often be connected directly at vertices without first producing complete triangular panels.

That allows the dome to grow as a network of members.

One strut connects to a hub.

Another strut connects to the next hub.

As more pieces are added, the triangular pattern begins locking the structure into its intended form.

During this stage, the partially assembled frame may still be flexible.

Fasteners may be left slightly loose so the geometry can settle into position before final tightening.

Temporary supports or bracing may also be needed depending on the assembly sequence.

The connection system has to allow enough practical movement for assembly without relying on uncontrolled looseness as part of the finished structural design.

SAFETY / ENGINEERING

A hub is not just a positioning device.

In a finished structure, it is part of the load path.

Forces moving through one strut have to pass through the connection and into neighboring members.

That means hub plates, bolts, screws, welds, timber around holes, edge distances, washers, bearing surfaces, and connection geometry can all matter structurally.

A connection that successfully holds the pieces together during assembly is not automatically adequate for a permanent occupied structure.

The required connection capacity depends on the structure, loads, materials, fasteners, geometry, and applicable building requirements.

This book does not assign structural capacity to a hub simply because the parts can be assembled.

WHY THE WEDGE METHOD TAKES A DIFFERENT APPROACH

The wedge method starts from the same geometric problem but changes where some of that geometry is handled.

Traditional strut-and-hub construction can keep a rectangular strut simple and place more of the three-dimensional connection problem into the hub.

The wedge method moves part of that problem into the timber member itself.

Instead of using only a rectangular cross-section and asking the connector to accommodate the entire change between neighboring faces, the timber is shaped so that its interior and exterior widths are different.

The wedge therefore participates in the face-to-face transition.

This does not automatically eliminate every plate, bolt, screw, or connector.

It also does not mean that hubs are a bad solution.

They are simply a different way of dividing the same geometric problem.

We can think of the two approaches like this:

Traditional strut/hub construction:

$$
\text{simple member} + \text{specialized vertex connection}
$$

Wedge construction:

$$
\text{geometry-shaped member} + \text{connection adapted to that member}
$$

That distinction is central to the rest of this book.

The question is not whether a dome needs connection geometry.

It does.

The question is where we choose to put that geometry.

We can concentrate more of it in a hub.

We can shape more of it into the timber.

Or we can build a hybrid system that uses both.

Understanding traditional hub construction first makes the wedge method easier to understand, because both systems are solving the same physical problem from different directions.

sections.title: Panelized domes
sections.body:
A geodesic dome does not have to be built as a loose frame first and skinned later.

Another approach is to build the dome from panels.

A panelized dome treats each triangular face, or sometimes groups of faces, as a prefabricated building unit.

Instead of assembling only struts and hubs, the builder assembles complete sections that already contain some combination of frame, sheathing, insulation, weather barrier, interior finish, or connection hardware.

That changes the entire workflow.

A strut-built dome starts with lines.

A panelized dome starts with surfaces.

DESIGN VARIATION

The simplest triangular panel might be nothing more than a sheet cut to the shape of one geodesic face.

A more developed panel might contain:

* structural edge members,
* an exterior skin,
* insulation,
* an interior skin,
* gasket material,
* attachment hardware,
* window openings,
* or service penetrations.

At that point the triangle is no longer just geometry.

It becomes a prefabricated wall or roof section.

The same basic geodesic layout is still underneath everything.

The triangle dimensions still come from the dome geometry.

The difference is that more construction work happens before the panel reaches the dome.

That can be useful when repeatability matters.

If twenty panels share the same geometry, the builder can make one accurate jig and use it repeatedly.

If several panel types exist, each type can have its own fixture, cut list, and assembly process.

The manufacturing problem becomes:

Make Panel A correctly.

Make Panel B correctly.

Make however many of each type the dome requires.

Then assemble those panels in the correct pattern.

PANEL GEOMETRY STILL COMES FIRST

A panel cannot be designed correctly until the triangular face underneath it is known.

For each panel type we eventually need to know:

* the three edge lengths,
* the three internal angles,
* the orientation of the panel in the dome,
* the angle between that panel and its neighbors,
* the connection method along each edge,
* and how the panel thickness relates to the intended dome surface.

This is especially important when the panel is thick.

A flat sheet has an inside face and an outside face that are close together.

A thick insulated panel may move the exterior skin noticeably farther from the theoretical geodesic chord.

If neighboring panels are simply made from the same two-dimensional triangle and pushed together, the exterior edges may not meet the way the builder expects.

The edge geometry has to account for thickness.

That can mean bevels, wedges, gaskets, external covers, internal battens, or another joint system.

This is the same three-dimensional problem seen in strut construction.

We have just moved it into the panel edge.

FRAME-FIRST PANELS

One panelized method is to build a triangular timber frame first.

The three edge members define the panel.

Sheathing is then attached to that frame.

The frame may be built from rectangular lumber, wedge-shaped lumber, laminated members, or another section.

This approach gives the panel its own structural border before it reaches the dome.

In a wedge-method system, the wedge can become part of that panel edge.

Instead of using a rectangular perimeter and then cutting a separate bevel into the panel connection, the timber edge itself can help establish the transition between neighboring faces.

That creates a useful manufacturing possibility:

The wedge strut can act as both a structural member and a panel-edge geometry component.

The panel skin can then be attached to the outside of the triangular frame.

When two complete panels are brought together, their wedge-shaped edge members meet at the dome joint.

The connection system then has to clamp, screw, bolt, plate, or otherwise join those edges in a controlled way.

SKIN-FIRST PANELS

Another method starts with the sheet material.

A triangular panel is cut first and framing is attached behind it.

This may be practical for thin sheathing or lightweight assemblies where the skin itself provides the easiest reference surface during fabrication.

The advantage is that the visible panel shape can be controlled directly from a template or CNC layout.

The disadvantage is that the rear framing still has to agree with the three-dimensional joint geometry.

A flat triangle is easy to cut.

Making many thick flat triangles close into a dome without gaps is the harder part.

That is why panel edge design matters as much as panel face dimensions.

PANEL JOINTS

When panels meet, several things have to happen at once.

The joint has to:

* locate the panels,
* hold them together,
* deal with the angle between faces,
* control water entry,
* control air leakage where required,
* allow whatever installation tolerance the system needs,
* and transfer structural forces if the panel is part of the load-bearing system.

One connection may not need to do every job by itself.

For example, a structural fastener might hold the panels together while a separate gasket handles weather sealing.

An exterior cap might cover the seam.

An interior batten might reinforce it.

A removable design might use bolts or clamps instead of permanent adhesive.

The important part is to stop treating "the panel joint" as one vague detail.

It is several problems occupying the same edge.

PANELIZATION AND REPEATABILITY

Panel construction makes the most sense when we take advantage of repetition.

If every panel is built differently in the field, much of the benefit disappears.

The useful approach is to identify the repeating panel families early.

For each family we can eventually create:

* a panel ID,
* a drawing,
* a cut list,
* a jig,
* an edge orientation,
* an assembly sequence,
* and a location map for the finished dome.

That turns the dome into something closer to a manufactured kit.

The site work becomes assembly of previously defined parts instead of fabrication of every part in place.

This does not automatically make the project faster.

The fabrication time still exists.

It has simply moved into a more controlled stage of the build.

The advantage is that repeatable work can be organized around fixtures, templates, stops, and inspection.

A bad first panel can be corrected before twenty more are made from the same setup.

A good setup can then be repeated without re-solving the geometry each time.

OPENINGS AND SPECIAL PANELS

Doors and windows interrupt the repeating triangle system.

A panelized dome gives us one way to handle that interruption.

Instead of modifying random pieces during erection, special panels can be designed before assembly.

For example:

* one triangular panel could contain a window,
* several neighboring triangles could be replaced by a reinforced door module,
* one panel could contain a ventilation opening,
* or a utility panel could contain controlled service penetrations.

These special pieces should be treated as separate panel types.

They may look similar to the normal panels from outside, but structurally and functionally they are not the same.

That means they need their own drawings and connection details.

A hole cut into a completed generic panel is not automatically equivalent to a panel designed around that opening.

REMOVABLE PANELS

DESIGN VARIATION

Panelization also makes removable sections possible.

If the joint system is mechanical rather than permanently bonded, an individual panel could potentially be removed for repair, replacement, modification, or access.

That could be useful for:

* replacing damaged exterior sections,
* changing transparent and opaque panels,
* adding future openings,
* accessing utilities,
* or experimenting with different enclosure systems on the same structural frame.

This idea becomes more useful when panel dimensions and connections are standardized.

If every panel is custom-fit during construction, replacing one later may require rebuilding that exact piece by hand.

If the panel system is repeatable, replacement becomes a manufacturing problem rather than a reconstruction problem.

That does not mean every structural panel should be casually removable.

If the panel participates in the load path, removing it may change the behavior of the structure.

The connection between structural frame and removable shell therefore needs to be clearly defined.

SEPARATING FRAME FROM SHELL

One useful design decision is whether the panel is part of the structure or only part of the enclosure.

Those are two different systems.

In one version, the dome has a complete timber frame.

Panels attach to that frame but are not intended to be the primary structural system.

In another version, the panel and its perimeter framing act together as a structural module.

In another, the skin itself may participate in transferring forces between the edges.

Those systems may look similar after the dome is finished.

They should not be assumed to behave the same way.

For the wedge method, separating the frame and shell can keep the basic structural concept easier to understand.

The wedge members establish the geodesic frame.

The panel system then attaches to that frame.

Later variations can explore whether the panel can take on additional structural work.

SAFETY / ENGINEERING

A panel that carries structural load needs more than correct triangle dimensions.

Its behavior can depend on:

* panel material,
* thickness,
* edge framing,
* fastener spacing,
* connection design,
* openings,
* moisture,
* buckling,
* wind pressure,
* suction,
* and the way forces enter and leave the panel.

For that reason, this book does not treat a panel as structural simply because it fits into the geodesic pattern.

A panel can be geometrically correct and still be structurally inadequate.

Geometry tells us where the piece belongs.

Engineering determines what that piece can safely carry.

REFERENCE BUILD

For the 20-foot 2V reference dome, panelization will eventually be tied directly to the verified triangle families.

Once those triangle types are fixed, each repeated face can be assigned a panel type.

A basic workflow will be:

1. identify the verified triangle families,
2. assign a panel ID to each family,
3. determine the edge geometry,
4. determine how panel thickness relates to the theoretical dome surface,
5. design the joint between neighboring panels,
6. define normal and special panels,
7. create fabrication jigs or templates,
8. label the panels,
9. assemble them according to a dome map.

That gives us a panel schedule instead of a pile of triangles.

The important idea is that panelization does not replace the dome geometry.

It packages the geometry into larger, repeatable building units.

sections.title: Where the wedge method differs
sections.body:
The wedge method changes where the dome's three-dimensional geometry is handled.

A conventional timber dome often starts with rectangular struts and then uses hubs, plates, brackets, compound end cuts, or other connection hardware to make those rectangular members meet correctly in space.

The wedge method moves part of that problem into the member itself.

Instead of treating every strut as a rectangular stick with parallel inside and outside faces, the timber is shaped so the inside edge is narrower than the outside edge.

The member becomes part of the angular transition between neighboring triangular faces.

That is the main difference.

The dome still depends on correct geodesic geometry.

The struts still have to be the correct lengths.

The vertices still have to occur in the correct locations.

The triangles still have to assemble into the intended spherical pattern.

The wedge does not replace any of that.

It changes how the physical timber occupies the geometry.

GEOMETRY

A geodesic frame can be thought of as a network of theoretical straight lines joining vertices.

Those lines are the chord geometry.

A conventional rectangular strut is then placed along one of those lines. Its cross-section does not naturally change from the interior side of the dome to the exterior side.

That means the joint has to handle the difference in direction between the triangular face on one side and the triangular face on the other.

A wedge-shaped member gives us another way to handle that transition.

Viewed in cross-section, the member has an interior width and an exterior width.

The two side faces are therefore not parallel.

That creates an included wedge angle.

If the difference between the outside width and inside width is:

$$
\Delta w = w_{outside}-w_{inside}
$$

and the distance between the interior and exterior reference faces is \(t\), then a symmetrical wedge can be described by:

$$
\alpha = 2\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\Delta w}{2t}\right)
$$

where:

* \(\alpha\) is the total included wedge angle,
* \(w_{outside}\) is the outside width,
* \(w_{inside}\) is the inside width,
* and \(t\) is the thickness between the inside and outside reference faces.

This equation describes the shape of the wedge.

It does not tell us automatically what wedge angle a particular dome needs.

That angle depends on the actual dome geometry, the reference line used through the timber, the relationship between neighboring faces, and the connection method.

The important part is that the timber now contains a controlled angular relationship in its own cross-section.

RECTANGULAR MEMBER VERSUS WEDGE MEMBER

Take two neighboring triangular faces.

If their common edge is made from a rectangular timber, the member has approximately the same width at the inside and outside of the frame.

The two triangular faces still need to turn relative to one another.

That change may be handled with a gap, bevel, plate, hub, bracket, angled fastener arrangement, or some combination of those.

Now replace that rectangular member with a wedge.

The inside edge is narrower.

The outside edge is wider.

The widening cross-section gives the adjoining faces more separation toward the exterior while allowing them to remain closer together toward the interior.

Instead of asking the connection to create the entire face-to-face transition, some of that geometry is already built into the timber.

That is the central construction idea behind the wedge method.

The member is not only spanning from one vertex to another.

Its cross-section is also doing geometric work.

THE WEDGE IS NOT A HUB

It would be easy to describe the system simply as hubless construction, but that description can be misleading.

Removing a traditional central hub does not remove the need for a connection.

The members still have to be held together.

The vertex still has to stay in the correct location.

Loads still have to pass from one member into the others.

The difference is that a large specialized hub does not necessarily have to establish the primary angular relationship between the surrounding faces.

Depending on the version of the system, the remaining connection could use:

* structural screws,
* through-bolts,
* washers,
* internal plates,
* external plates,
* straps,
* brackets,
* direct timber contact,
* or combinations of these.

The wedge method therefore redistributes the geometry rather than eliminating connection design.

Some of the work normally done by a hub is moved into the timber.

THE MEMBER BECOMES A REPEATED GEOMETRIC PART

This changes the fabrication problem.

In a traditional hub system, the strut can often remain a relatively simple component while the specialized hub handles more of the spatial geometry.

In the wedge method, the strut becomes a more specialized component.

That means its manufacturing process matters.

If one wedge profile is correct, we want to reproduce that profile instead of laying out every part independently.

A practical production process should eventually define:

* the starting stock,
* the reference face,
* the fence or jig position,
* the workholding method,
* the order of cuts,
* the final length reference,
* the drilling reference,
* the labeling method,
* and the inspection method.

The goal is to stop treating each wedge as a custom carving.

It should become a manufactured part.

If twenty members are supposed to be identical, the twentieth member should come from the same references and setup as the first.

That is where jigs, fences, stops, templates, and gauges become more useful than repeated measuring.

FABRICATION ERRORS

The wedge creates another set of dimensions that have to remain controlled.

A rectangular strut can be the correct length and still have minor width variation without completely changing its basic geometry.

With a wedge, the width relationship is part of the intended shape.

If the outside width changes while the inside width stays the same, the wedge angle changes.

If the timber is flipped during assembly, the taper works in the opposite direction.

If the wrong face becomes the reference during a cutting operation, the same mistake can be reproduced across an entire batch.

The common errors therefore need to be kept separate:

* incorrect strut length,
* incorrect inside width,
* incorrect outside width,
* incorrect wedge angle,
* reversed wedge orientation,
* incorrect end geometry,
* incorrect fastener-hole position,
* incorrect member family,
* and incorrect labeling.

These errors do not all produce the same result.

A wrong strut length changes the vertex position.

A wrong wedge profile changes how the surrounding faces meet.

A reversed wedge puts the wide side toward the interior instead of the exterior.

A misplaced bolt hole can change the effective connection point even when the overall piece of timber is the correct length.

This means quality control eventually has to check more than one measurement.

BUILD NOTE

The actual reference-build fabrication procedure should be recorded from the shop rather than invented from the geometry.

For each wedge family, that record should include:

* nominal starting stock,
* actual measured stock dimensions,
* tool used,
* fence or guide setup,
* workholding,
* first cut,
* second cut if required,
* reference face after each cut,
* final length operation,
* drilling operation,
* labeling,
* target dimensions,
* measured finished dimensions,
* and variation across multiple completed parts.

Until those measurements exist, the book can explain how the operation should be organized without claiming a production tolerance that has not been measured.

The same rule applies to saw settings.

A drawing can show the intended wedge.

The builder-facing procedure needs the actual setup used to reproduce it.

DIMENSIONAL LUMBER

One version of the wedge method starts with ordinary rectangular lumber.

The wedge profile is ripped from that rectangular blank.

The cutting layout matters because the offcut may represent a large portion of the original board.

That does not automatically mean the offcut is waste.

Depending on the final wedge geometry, another useful member may be recovered from it.

The same material might produce:

* another wedge,
* a smaller structural member,
* blocking,
* panel cleats,
* spacers,
* trim,
* or another repeated component.

This makes material yield part of the system.

The fastest way to produce one wedge is not necessarily the most efficient way to process all the lumber required for a dome.

The better question is how many useful finished parts can be recovered from each starting board while maintaining repeatable reference surfaces.

LOGS AND LARGER TIMBER

The wedge method also creates another possibility when the starting material is a log or large timber.

A log is already radial in cross-section.

Instead of converting the entire log into rectangular boards first, the log can potentially be divided longitudinally into rough wedge-like sectors.

Those sectors can then be processed into controlled structural members.

This does not mean that a raw radial slice from a tree is automatically a finished dome strut.

The original log may have:

* taper,
* sweep,
* knots,
* checks,
* changing diameter,
* moisture variation,
* irregular grain,
* and irregular exterior surfaces.

The rough wedge still needs controlled reference surfaces and verified dimensions.

But the material layout can change substantially.

Instead of:

$$
\text{log} \rightarrow \text{rectangular lumber} \rightarrow \text{wedge}
$$

the process can potentially become:

$$
\text{log} \rightarrow \text{rough wedge sectors} \rightarrow \text{finished wedges}
$$

That is more than a different connection detail.

It changes how the structural material can be recovered from the original timber.

CONNECTION GEOMETRY STILL MATTERS

Shaping the member can reduce how much specialized three-dimensional geometry has to be concentrated at the vertex.

It does not make the connection trivial.

The connection still has to answer practical questions.

Where is the theoretical vertex?

Where is the fastener center?

Which timber surfaces actually touch?

Are the wedges clamped directly together?

Is there a controlled gap?

Does a plate bridge several members?

Can the connection be tightened after erection?

Can a damaged member be replaced?

Does an exterior panel attach across the same joint?

How does the connection affect the physical cut length compared with the theoretical chord?

Those questions connect the wedge profile to the actual building system.

The two problems therefore have to be developed together:

$$
\text{member geometry}
$$

and

$$
\text{connection geometry}
$$

A good wedge profile attached through a poorly defined connection is not a complete system.

Neither is a good connection attached to incorrectly manufactured wedges.

REPEATABILITY IS THE LARGER IDEA

The wedge is the obvious visual difference, but repeatability is the more important fabrication idea behind the method.

A dome may contain a large number of pieces while containing only a relatively small number of unique part families.

Once those families are defined, each one can eventually have:

* a profile,
* a length,
* a drilling pattern,
* a label,
* a manufacturing fixture,
* an inspection gauge,
* and a known location in the finished dome.

That changes the question during assembly.

Instead of asking:

"How do I make this piece fit here?"

we should be asking:

"Which defined part belongs here, and was that part made correctly?"

That difference matters.

Custom fitting allows one error to be hidden by another adjustment.

Repeatable fabrication makes the error easier to find.

If a correctly labeled part does not fit where the geometry says it belongs, something is wrong with the part, the assembly position, the connection, or the underlying model.

That gives us a system that can be checked instead of continuously improvised.

DESIGN VARIATION

The wedge concept can also extend into panelized construction.

A wedge member can form the perimeter of a triangular panel.

The outside face of the wedge can support exterior sheathing while the inside edge defines the interior side of the frame.

Neighboring wedge-framed panels can then meet along their prepared edges.

That creates the possibility of prefabricating larger triangular modules instead of assembling every individual strut on site.

Other versions could keep the wedge frame permanent while making the exterior panel removable.

Still others could combine the wedge with metal reinforcement or laminated timber.

These are variations of the same underlying idea: make the member participate in the dome geometry instead of requiring every spatial relationship to be created entirely by separate hardware.

SAFETY / ENGINEERING

Changing the member shape does not prove structural capacity.

The wedge affects the physical cross-section of the timber and may also affect:

* fastener placement,
* available edge distance,
* bearing surfaces,
* connection geometry,
* bending orientation,
* and the amount of wood remaining at different parts of the section.

Those effects have to be evaluated for the actual material, joint, and loading condition.

A wedge that fits the geometry correctly is not automatically a structurally adequate wedge.

The same applies to log-derived members.

Material efficiency does not override timber quality, grading, defects, moisture, connection requirements, or structural analysis.

The geometry tells us what shape we are trying to build.

Engineering determines whether the resulting parts and connections can carry the required loads.

WHERE THE METHOD DIFFERS

The wedge method differs from conventional timber geodesic construction in several connected ways.

It makes the shape of the timber part of the three-dimensional dome geometry.

It can reduce the amount of specialized geometry concentrated in a traditional hub.

It turns cross-sectional accuracy into part of the fabrication process.

It can be produced from rectangular lumber, larger sawn timber, or potentially timber recovered directly from logs.

It can form the edge geometry of prefabricated triangular panels.

Most importantly, it gives us a system that can be broken into defined and repeatable manufacturing operations.

That is the point where the wedge stops being only a shape.

It becomes a building method.

sections.title: Basic concept
sections.body:
The wedge method starts with one simple change:

Instead of building the dome from rectangular struts and solving most of the three-dimensional geometry at the joints, we shape the struts so the timber itself participates in the dome geometry.

That is the core idea.

A normal rectangular board has approximately the same width on its inside and outside faces.

A wedge-shaped member does not.

Its narrow side faces toward the interior of the dome.

Its wider side faces toward the exterior.

When those members are arranged into triangles, the changing width of the wedge helps neighboring triangular faces turn relative to one another.

The member is therefore doing two jobs at once.

It spans between vertices.

It also helps establish the angular relationship between the faces on either side of it.

GEOMETRY

The theoretical geodesic frame can still be represented as straight chord lines connecting vertices.

The wedge does not replace those chord lines.

It is built around them.

That distinction is useful because it lets us separate the geometry into two layers.

The first layer is the mathematical dome.

That layer tells us:

* where the vertices are,
* which vertices connect,
* the chord lengths,
* the triangle families,
* and the face-to-face relationships.

The second layer is the physical timber.

That layer tells us:

* how wide the member is on the inside,
* how wide it is on the outside,
* how thick it is,
* how it is oriented,
* where the fasteners pass through it,
* and how neighboring members actually meet.

The wedge method works when those two layers agree.

If the theoretical dome is correct but the wedge profile is wrong, the physical frame will not follow the intended geometry correctly.

If the wedge profile is correct but the strut lengths are wrong, the vertices will be misplaced.

Both parts matter.

THE WEDGE ORIENTATION

The basic orientation is:

narrow side inward,

wide side outward.

This should remain visually obvious during fabrication and assembly.

The reason is geometric.

The interior side of the dome is closer to the center of the sphere.

The exterior side is farther from the center.

As neighboring triangular faces wrap around the dome, they spread apart toward the exterior.

The wedge shape gives us a member whose cross-section follows that general relationship.

A reversed wedge works against the intended orientation.

If a member is installed wide-side inward and narrow-side outward, it is not merely cosmetically reversed.

Its cross-section is now pointing in the wrong direction relative to the dome.

That is why every finished member should eventually have an obvious inside/outside marking.

A simple label, arrow, burn mark, paint mark, stamped letter, or other repeatable identifier can prevent an orientation error during assembly.

THE TRIANGLE STILL CONTROLS THE FRAME

The wedge does not make the dome by itself.

The triangles do.

The strut lengths still define the triangle edges.

The triangle geometry still determines the shape of each flat face.

The wedge then helps those faces meet in three dimensions.

This distinction should stay clear throughout the book.

A wedge angle is not a substitute for the correct triangle.

A correct triangle does not automatically tell us the correct wedge profile.

And the correct wedge profile does not automatically tell us the correct connection.

We can treat those as three linked design problems:

$$
\text{triangle geometry}
$$

$$
\text{wedge geometry}
$$

$$
\text{connection geometry}
$$

The complete system comes from making all three agree.

ONE MEMBER, TWO NEIGHBORING FACES

Each wedge member can be thought of as lying along the shared edge between two neighboring triangular faces.

One face exists on one side of the strut.

Another face exists on the other side.

Those faces are not normally coplanar.

They meet at an angle.

That means the edge between them has to work in three dimensions.

A rectangular member gives both sides approximately parallel reference faces.

A wedge member gives the two sides a controlled divergence between the interior and exterior.

That is the physical feature we are trying to use.

The wedge is therefore best understood from a cross-section perpendicular to the strut length.

Looking only at the long side of the timber can hide the entire concept.

From the side, the wedge may look like an ordinary straight board.

From the end, the difference becomes obvious.

That end view should be used repeatedly throughout this book.

VERTICES

A dome vertex is where several struts meet.

The number of members depends on the location and the geometry.

Some vertices may have five members meeting.

Others may have six.

Boundary conditions can create other arrangements.

The wedge method does not eliminate those vertex patterns.

It changes the shapes of the members entering them.

At a vertex, several wedge-shaped struts approach from different directions.

The connection must still locate those members correctly and hold them together.

The wedge profile helps the surrounding faces occupy the correct spatial relationship, but the vertex still needs a practical connection system.

That connection might be very simple.

It might not be.

The final detail depends on how the member ends are cut, how much timber remains around the fasteners, whether the members contact one another directly, whether plates are used, and where the theoretical vertex lies relative to the physical wood.

For that reason, the vertex should be thought of as an assembly of several controlled parts rather than a point where we simply force the lumber together.

THREE-MEMBER RELATIONSHIPS

Before thinking about a full five-way or six-way vertex, it is useful to reduce the problem.

Take three members and build one triangle.

Now the basic relationships are visible.

Each member has:

* a length,
* an inside face,
* an outside face,
* a left side,
* a right side,
* and two ends.

That orientation needs to remain consistent.

If the triangle is assembled correctly, the narrow faces point toward the interior side of the future dome.

The wider faces point toward the exterior.

That triangle becomes one flat face of the larger structure.

Add another triangle along one of its edges and the three-dimensional relationship becomes easier to see.

The shared wedge member sits between the two faces.

Repeat this around the structure and the dome emerges.

This is a useful way to think about assembly because the complete vertex can look complicated while the individual relationships remain simple.

Start with one member.

Then one triangle.

Then two neighboring triangles.

Then the complete vertex.

Then the dome.

That sequence keeps the geometry understandable.

THE WEDGE PROFILE

A finished wedge member can be described with a small group of dimensions.

At minimum, we need:

* inside width,
* outside width,
* thickness,
* length,
* and end geometry.

If holes or other connection features are added, we also need:

* hole diameter,
* hole location,
* edge distance,
* and reference surface.

Those dimensions define the physical part.

A basic symmetric wedge cross-section can be described by:

$$
\Delta w = w_{outside}-w_{inside}
$$

where:

* \(w_{outside}\) is the exterior width,
* \(w_{inside}\) is the interior width.

If the taper is symmetric about the member centerline, each side accounts for half of that difference:

$$
\frac{\Delta w}{2}
$$

If \(t\) is the distance from the inside face to the outside face, one side taper angle is:

$$
\beta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\Delta w/2}{t}\right)
$$

and the total included wedge angle is:

$$
\alpha=2\beta
$$

or:

$$
\alpha=2\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\Delta w}{2t}\right)
$$

This gives us a way to describe a finished wedge once the required widths and thickness are known.

It does not yet tell us what those dimensions should be for the reference dome.

That has to come from the verified dome and joint geometry.

MANUFACTURING LOGIC

Once a wedge profile is established, it should become a repeatable shop operation.

The goal is not:

measure a strange shape,

cut it,

check whether it fits,

then adjust the next one.

The goal is:

define the part,

define the process,

repeat the process.

That may mean a fence setting.

It may mean a dedicated sled.

It may mean a taper jig.

It may mean splitting or ripping larger stock along predetermined lines.

It may mean using one finished surface as the datum for every later operation.

The actual production method can vary.

The principle should not.

Every repeatable dimension should come from a repeatable reference.

That becomes especially important when the dome requires many parts.

A small error repeated once may be manageable.

A small error repeated forty times becomes a pattern.

BUILD NOTE

The builder-facing version of this method should eventually record the actual production setup.

For the reference build, that means documenting:

* the stock used,
* actual measured stock dimensions,
* cutting tool,
* jig or fence arrangement,
* feed direction,
* workholding,
* cut order,
* datum surface,
* final length operation,
* drilling operation,
* marking method,
* and measured variation between finished parts.

Those details should come from the actual fabrication process.

Until they are measured, they remain development work rather than finished production specifications.

MATERIAL DOES NOT HAVE TO START AS A BOARD

The wedge shape can be produced from different starting materials.

One method starts with dimensional lumber and removes material until the required cross-section remains.

Another can begin with larger sawn timber.

Another can begin with a log and recover wedge-like sectors directly from the original round material.

The finished requirement is the same:

the structural member must end up with controlled geometry.

How we reach that geometry can change.

This gives the wedge method an important manufacturing flexibility.

The geometric part is defined first.

The raw material strategy can then be chosen based on what is available.

DESIGN VARIATION

A wedge can also become more than a bare strut.

It can become the edge of a triangular panel.

It can be laminated from several pieces.

It can be reinforced with metal.

It can include a groove, rabbet, panel seat, gasket channel, or other feature.

It can be produced as part of a larger prefabricated module.

Those variations should all be treated as later branches of the basic system.

The simplest version is still the best place to start:

a straight structural member,

with a controlled wedge-shaped cross-section,

oriented narrow-side inward and wide-side outward,

placed along a verified geodesic edge,

and connected to the neighboring wedge members at the correct vertices.

REFERENCE BUILD

For the 20-foot-diameter 2V reference dome, we will eventually reduce the structure to a defined set of member families.

Each family will need:

* a verified chord relationship,
* a physical cut length,
* a wedge profile,
* an orientation,
* a connection pattern,
* a quantity,
* and a label.

Those values should not be mixed together prematurely.

First the exact 2V geometry must be frozen.

Then the connection reference has to be defined.

Then the wedge profile can be derived around that system.

Once those decisions are fixed, the book can move from concept to a real shop table.

That table should eventually allow a builder to look at a member labeled, for example, "A," and know exactly what that means:

which stock to start with,

which wedge profile to cut,

how long to make it,

where to drill it,

which direction faces inward,

and where it belongs in the dome.

That is the basic concept of the wedge method in practical terms.

Turn the geometry into defined parts.

Turn the defined parts into repeatable operations.

Then assemble those operations back into the dome.
